 WhatsApp Economy Explained: Is the RBI hiking rates without changing the repo?
 By : Latha Venkatesh October 27, 2026 | 16:20 IST Published On Oct 27, 2026 | 16:20 IST 
 Last Updated On Oct 27, 2026 | 16:20 IST 
 Twitter 
 Whatsapp 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Copy Link 
 Summary Overnight borrowing costs have risen above the repo rate as tighter liquidity pushes up money market rates. What does this mean for loans, bond yields, inflation and the rupee?
 + Follow on Google Add as preferred source India's overnight borrowing costs have risen over the past two weeks, with the interbank call rate climbing above the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) repo rate of 5.5%.
 The RBI has not announced another policy rate hike, but tighter liquidity is pushing up borrowing costs across money markets. This raises a key question: Is the RBI tightening monetary conditions without formally raising the repo rate?
 What is driving the rise in overnight borrowing costs? 
 The interbank call rate, at which banks lend to and borrow from one another for a day, rose to around 5.9% from 5.65% last week. It has remained above the RBI's 5.5% repo rate since around October 14, pointing to tighter access to short-term funds.
 Normally, the RBI manages overnight rates through a corridor defined by the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) and the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF). Tighter liquidity has pushed overnight borrowing costs close to the upper end of that corridor.
 Why is liquidity tightening? 
 Several factors are draining funds from the banking system. The RBI's dollar sales to support the rupee absorb rupee liquidity, while higher cash withdrawals ahead of Diwali and GST payments can also reduce funds available with banks.
 The RBI has injected money through repo and variable rate repo operations, but banks have repeatedly bid for more funds than the central bank has offered.
 For example: 
 On October 19, banks sought around ₹1.5 lakh crore, while the RBI supplied ₹1 lakh crore.
 On October 22, banks bid for ₹1.62 lakh crore, but the RBI injected only ₹50,000 crore.
 On October 26, banks demanded ₹1.86 lakh crore, while the RBI provided ₹1.5 lakh crore.
 As a result, banks have increasingly borrowed from each other at higher rates, pushing up the overnight call rate.
 What does this mean for interest rates? 
 Higher overnight funding costs are already feeding into other parts of the fixed-income market.
 Commercial paper yields for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) have risen from about 7.85% in mid-October to around 8.4%. Overnight Indexed Swap (OIS) rates have also increased by roughly 30-60 basis points across different maturities.
 These movements suggest that markets are factoring in tighter financial conditions, with borrowing costs rising despite no further formal repo rate hike.
 Why might the RBI be tightening liquidity? 
 One possible explanation is that tighter liquidity is helping the RBI manage pressure on the rupee while responding to inflation risks. Crude oil prices have climbed from around $100-105 a barrel to about $115, raising concerns about inflation.
 The RBI Governor said in an October 14 interview that rate hikes could be used to maintain financial stability, including currency stability. The RBI's October 7 Monetary Policy Report also said liquidity management would depend on domestic financial conditions, policy decisions and the monetary policy stance.
 These signals provide context for the view the RBI may be effectively delivering a second rate hike through liquidity management, pushing up borrowing costs without formally changing the repo rate.
